desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

Cut the list into two lists in the middle. The first list gets the first ceil(n / 2) nodes and the second list gets the remaining floor(n / 2) nodes, both keeping their original order. Return [first, second], each given as an array of values.

For [1,2,3,4,5] the answer is [[1,2,3],[4,5]], and for [1,2,3,4] it is [[1,2],[3,4]]. In a real linked list you do not know n in advance, so try to find the cut in a single pass without counting the nodes first.
hints: Counting the nodes first and then walking n / 2 steps works. Can you locate the middle during a single walk?
Use two pointers that start at the head: slow moves one node per step and fast moves two nodes per step.
Stop when fast.next or fast.next.next is null. Then slow is the last node of the first half: the second list starts at slow.next, and you cut the link by setting slow.next = null.
editorial: The slow and fast pointer technique finds the middle in one pass. While fast can still jump two nodes, move slow by one and fast by two. When the loop ends, fast is at (or next to) the tail and slow has covered half of the distance, so it sits on the last node of the first half. For an even length the first half ends at the left of the two middle nodes, which gives exactly ceil(n / 2) nodes in the first part.

Cut the list by saving second = slow.next and setting slow.next = null. The scan is O(n) time and uses O(1) extra pointers. This split is the first step of merge sort on a linked list and of the palindrome check.
